How long does it take to learn Japanese for beginners?

The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. However, the amount of time it takes to learn Japanese for beginners depends on various factors, such as how often and how long you study, the quality of your study materials, your motivation, and your natural ability to learn languages.
How many hours a day should I study Japanese to become fluent?

The number of hours a day you need to study Japanese to become fluent depends on your personal goals, your current level of proficiency, and your preferred learning style. Generally, it’s recommended to study at least 1-2 hours a day, every day, to make steady progress. As a reference, intensive Japanese courses typically 3 hours a day. Studying 6 hours or more in a day may lead to burnout.
Can I become fluent in Japanese in six months?

While it’s possible to make significant progress in six months of intensive study, becoming fully fluent in Japanese within such a short period is unlikely. Achieving fluency in Japanese requires a deep understanding of the language, which takes time to develop. You can achieve conversational fluency in six months.
How long does it take to pass the JLPT N5, N4, N3, N2 or N1 level?
On average, it takes 6 months to 1 year of dedicated study to pass each level of the JLPT. However, some people may take longer or shorter depending on their individual circumstances.
Can I learn Japanese faster with a tutor or language exchange partner?

Working with a tutor or language exchange partner can help you learn Japanese faster and more effectively. A tutor can provide personalized instruction and feedback, while a language exchange partner can offer opportunities to practice speaking and listening skills with a native speaker.
How long does it take to learn Japanese kanji?
On average, it takes about 2-3 years of consistent study to master the basic set of 2,136 Joyo kanji (commonly used characters in Japan).
Can I learn Japanese on my own without a teacher?

Yes, it’s possible to learn Japanese on your own without a teacher. However, self-study requires a lot of discipline, motivation, and the right resources. You’ll need to find quality textbooks, online resources, and study materials, and you’ll need to develop a consistent study routine to make progress.
Is it difficult to learn Japanese compared to other languages?

Japanese is considered to be a logical and consistent language with a relatively simple sound system, but it’s considered one of the hardest languages to learn for English speakers. FSI considered Japanese a “super-hard language”, categorizing it in the same group as Arabic, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese.

items.title: 10 Japanese Dad Jokes to Learn
items.author: Brian Trees
items.summary: Be warned: you are about to read the most groan-worthy Japanese dad jokes ever! 親父ギャグ (Oyaji gyagu), literally meaning “old man gags,” is the Japanese
items.text:
Be warned: you are about to read the most groan-worthy Japanese dad jokes ever! 親父ギャグ (Oyaji gyagu), literally meaning “old man gags,” is the Japanese equivalent of “dad jokes.” They are characterized by cheesy puns, or ダジャレ in Japanese. Similar to English, Japanese puns are built on homophones, or words that sound the same but have different meanings.

Dad jokes are just as cheesy in Japanese as they are in any language, but they are a great way to learn about Japanese culture and humor while practicing informal sentence structures. Japanese dad jokes can help with picking up natural language through their use of non-literal, figurative language.

What Are Japanese Dad Jokes or 親父ギャグ (Oyaji Gagu)?

Most Japanese dad jokes use homophones, a fancy grammatical term for when two different words, with different meanings, sound very similar. Since the Japanese language only has a limited number of unique syllables to build words from, homophones end up being very common, and it’s quite easy to make corny jokes out of them. This is the basis of many dad jokes and ダジャレ in general.

Onomatopoeia, or the written form of action sounds, are abundant in the Japanese language, so they are another common component of dad jokes.

1. このステーキはすてき！(kono suteeki wa suteki!)

Romaji: Kono suteeki wa suteki!
Meaning: The steak is wonderful!
Joke Explanation:
Steak → ステーキ (suteeki)
Wonderful → ステキ (suteki)

A classic, simple homophone that relies on nearly identical sounds, and the best part is that it only requires JLPT N5 knowledge to understand! ステーキ, meaning beef steak, a dad’s favorite food, is said quickly in a shortened form to sound just like ステキ, which means lovely or wonderful.

ステキな isn’t a very natural way to describe delicious food, so the intentional word choice elicits the inevitable groan. For natural, casual ways to describe food, you can combine the prefixes めちゃ or マジで, meaning very, with おいしい or うまい, meaning tasty.

2. 美味すぎて、馬になった。(umasugite, uma ni natta.)

Romaji: umasugite, uma ni natta
Meaning: It was so delicious I turned into a horse.
Joke Explanation:
Delicious → 美味い (umai)
Horse → 馬 (uma)

The pun comes from the similar sounds of 馬 (uma), meaning horse, and 美味い (umai), meaning “delicious.” The joke also incorporates a bit of N4 grammar: the suffix すぎる (sugiru), which means “too much.”

For example, if you want to emphasize how cold it is outside on the first day of winter, you may say さむすぎる instead of just さむい. The て form lets you connect clauses fluidly, showing cause and relation or the order of events. 馬 is the corresponding second homophone, followed by なった, the past tense form of なる, meaning to become.

3. 土管の中でドッカーン (Dokan no naka de dokkaan.)

Romaji: Dokan no naka de dokkaan.
Meaning: Kaboom inside the clay pipe.
Joke Explanation:
Clay Pipe → 土管 (dokan)
Kaboom →ドッカーン

This one is a combination effect of onomatopoeia with homophones. This joke that relies on more advanced kanji & vocabulary (around N1 level), using the very particular word for clay / earthen pipe土管 to sound like the onomatopoeia ドッカーン. A very simple N5 grammatical structure using の中で as a prepositional phrase, denoting where the kaboom took place. What makes this joke a bit more difficult is the advanced-level vocab 土管, which you will probably never encounter unless you read construction signs.

4. 餃子を食べて、仰天！(gyoza o tabete, gyoten!)

Romaji: gyoza o tabete, gyoten!
Meaning: I ate the gyoza and was amazed!
Joke Explanation:
Gyoza → 餃子
Amazed → 仰天 (gyoten)

This dad joke is a simple homophone that rhymes the popular Japanese dumplings, gyoza, with the expression of amazement, gyoten. Once again, we see the て- form grammar connecting the two clauses.

To read, this joke relies on more niche N3-level kanji knowledge. While 餃子 may be easier for foodies to recognize, 仰天 is quite advanced for learners. Still, this dad joke is easy to remember for your next visit to a Chinese restaurant!

5. チーターが池におっこちーたー. (Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.)

Romaji: Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.
Meaning: The cheetah fell into the pond.
Joke Explanation:
Cheetah → チーター
Fall down → 落っこちる (okkochiru)

This is more of an N2-level joke because the dramatized, colloquial form of 落ちる used in this joke isn’t commonly learned or taught early on. The rest of the rhyme uses easier vocabulary and grammar. We see が used once again as a subject particle, describing what the cheetah is doing. Combining this with the kanji for pond, 池, and using に as a preposition for the direction of the cheetah sets us up for the punchline.

The informal past tense of “to fall down” sounds just like the katakana word for cheetah, if dragged out, completing our homophonic dad joke. Once again, 落っこちる is more of a spoken, dramatized version of 落ちる

6. イルカはいるか？(iruka wa iruka?)

Romaji: Iruka wa iruka
Meaning: Are there any dolphins?
Joke Explanation:
Dolphin → イルカ
there is (living subject) → いる

This joke is as easy and cheesy as it gets. イルカ is written in katakana mainly because the kanji is hard to read, so it’s more convenient and accessible. は is used as our subject particle, as the dolphins are the subject of our silly question. いる, the word for “there is” when referring to animate subjects, is given the informal suffix か to turn it into a question. Maybe use this dad joke when you visit the Sumida Aquarium near Tokyo Skytree to test some reactions.

7. 車で、来るまで待つ。(kuruma de, kuru made matsu.)

Romaji: kuruma de kuru made matsu
Meaning: I will wait until they come by car.
Joke Explanation:
Car → 車 (kuruma)
Come → 来る (kuru)
Until → まで

Great for beginners to stretch their minds, this one uses a somewhat clever homophone, relying on the connection between 来る and まで to form the punchline. A phonetic mirror, if executed perfectly, 来るまで should sound just like 車 being enunciated poorly. 待つ is an N5-level vocabulary word meaning to wait. まで has several grammatical uses, but here it signifies waiting for the preceding action to occur.

8. 歯科医師が司会した。(shikaishi ga shikaishita)

Romaji: shikaishi ga shikaishita
Meaning: The dentist moderated the meeting
Joke Explanation:
Dentist → 歯科医師 (shikaishi)
Moderated → 司会する (shikai suru)

Because of the vocabulary it uses, this joke might be around N2 level. It’s structurally similar to the homophone examples we explained earlier, but it requires advanced kanji & vocab knowledge. This joke rests on the past tense of 司会する (shikaisuru), which is 司会した (shikaishita), meaning “led” or “moderated”.

To pull this dad joke off, you must pronounce 司会した (shikaishita) to sound exactly like 歯科医師 (shikaishita), which takes some over-enunciation of the し in した.

9. 電話に出んわ (Denwa ni denwa)

Romaji: denwa ni denwa
Meaning: I won’t answer the phone.
Explanation:
Phone → 電話 (denwa)
Answer → 出る (deru)

While the grammar and vocabulary are quite simple, the use of a different Japanese dialect could confuse beginners. This dad joke uses the Kansai dialect, which you may hear in Osaka or around Kyoto. The punchline of the joke takes the standard phrase 電話に出ない, dropping ない (nai) and adding ん (n), a shortened negative form, and the Kansai suffix わ, used to express emphasis. Now, 出ない sounds like denwa, similar to the word for “phone” or “call.”

In English, depending on where you learned to speak, we all say things a bit differently. The same applies to Japan, where different regions have their own way of saying things. One of the main alternatives to standard Japanese is the rough-sounding Kansai dialect.

10. 私はニューヨークで入浴した。(watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuuyokushita.)

Romaji: Watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuyokushita
Meaning: I took a bath in New York.
Explanation:
Bathing (formal) → 入浴 (nyuuyoku)
New York → ニューヨーク

Although this joke is grammatically simple, the term 入浴 (nyuuyoku) is very formal and uses old kanji that you will likely only see at an onsen. If you stretch out 入浴 (nyuuyoku), it sounds like how you would pronounce New York in katakana: ニューヨーク (nyuuyooku).

Combining these two homophones with the particle で, which denotes the location of the action, means the bath was taken in New York. Onsen are where you might see this kanji used seriously, for example: 入浴時間 (nyuuyoku jikan), meaning bathing hours.

How to Make Your Own Japanese Dad Jokes

Since these jokes are great practice for your Japanese skills no matter your level, consider playing around and writing your own. Here are a few easy steps to get you started.


Pay attention to homophones. Japanese’s limited number of unique syllables naturally creates many homophones.

Use simple grammar structures. These jokes don’t require difficult grammar, so don’t be afraid to form sentences informally.

Use what you know. This is the best way to master a language; using what you have learned in your own way will lead to a strong acquisition of Japanese.


Conclusion: Dad Jokes are Great for Practicing Japanese!

Once you get the hang of these puns, it is fun to use the vocab and grammar that you are familiar with to construct your own. This is a very basic one:

Salmon roe → いくら
How much? → いくら
いくらはいくら？
How much is the salmon roe?

Expressing your sense of humor is a huge part of language learning and speaking Japanese more naturally! Jokes aren’t only fun; they can help you remember more words and express yourself more freely without sticking to rigid, literal definitions!

Sharing a laugh may be one of the best ways to practice Japanese!

Learn to Express Your Sense of Humor with Coto Academy!

Showing your sense of humor is essential for natural Japanese fluency! Join our conversation-focused Japanese courses to learn to speak Japanese confidently and even joke around with friends! We offer flexible, part-time classes as well as intensive classes at a variety of levels.

Whether you’re starting from scratch or you want to take your Japanese to the next level, we have a class for you! Visit one of our campuses in Tokyo or Yokohama, or join online from anywhere around the world!

FAQ

What is oyaji gyagu?

親父ギャグ (oyaji gyagu) is the Japanese version of dad jokes. Literally meaning old man gag.

Why are dad jokes popular in Japan?

They originate from ancient poetry techniques and have been ingrained in modern comedy culture, with the added usefulness of their capability to break tension in stressful environments.

Can dad jokes help me learn Japanese?

Yes! They help you focus your listening skills for a language with so few syllables, and practice grammar by playing around with sentence structure.

Wonderful → ステキ (suteki)

A classic, simple homophone that relies on nearly identical sounds, and the best part is that it only requires JLPT N5 knowledge to understand! ステーキ, meaning beef steak, a dad’s favorite food, is said quickly in a shortened form to sound just like ステキ, which means lovely or wonderful.

ステキな isn’t a very natural way to describe delicious food, so the intentional word choice elicits the inevitable groan. For natural, casual ways to describe food, you can combine the prefixes めちゃ or マジで, meaning very, with おいしい or うまい, meaning tasty.
2. 美味すぎて、馬になった。(umasugite, uma ni natta.)

Romaji: umasugite, uma ni natta
Meaning: It was so delicious I turned into a horse.
Joke Explanation:
Delicious → 美味い (umai)
Horse → 馬 (uma)
The pun comes from the similar sounds of 馬 (uma), meaning horse, and 美味い (umai), meaning “delicious.” The joke also incorporates a bit of N4 grammar: the suffix すぎる (sugiru), which means “too much.”

For example, if you want to emphasize how cold it is outside on the first day of winter, you may say さむすぎる instead of just さむい. The て form lets you connect clauses fluidly, showing cause and relation or the order of events. 馬 is the corresponding second homophone, followed by なった, the past tense form of なる, meaning to become.
3. 土管の中でドッカーン (Dokan no naka de dokkaan.)

Romaji: Dokan no naka de dokkaan.
Meaning: Kaboom inside the clay pipe.
Joke Explanation:
Clay Pipe → 土管 (dokan)
Kaboom →ドッカーン

This one is a combination effect of onomatopoeia with homophones. This joke that relies on more advanced kanji & vocabulary (around N1 level), using the very particular word for clay / earthen pipe土管 to sound like the onomatopoeia ドッカーン. A very simple N5 grammatical structure using の中で as a prepositional phrase, denoting where the kaboom took place. What makes this joke a bit more difficult is the advanced-level vocab 土管, which you will probably never encounter unless you read construction signs.
4. 餃子を食べて、仰天！(gyoza o tabete, gyoten!)

Romaji: gyoza o tabete, gyoten!
Meaning: I ate the gyoza and was amazed!
Joke Explanation:
Gyoza → 餃子
Amazed → 仰天 (gyoten)
This dad joke is a simple homophone that rhymes the popular Japanese dumplings, gyoza, with the expression of amazement, gyoten. Once again, we see the て- form grammar connecting the two clauses.

To read, this joke relies on more niche N3-level kanji knowledge. While 餃子 may be easier for foodies to recognize, 仰天 is quite advanced for learners. Still, this dad joke is easy to remember for your next visit to a Chinese restaurant!
5. チーターが池におっこちーたー. (Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.)

Romaji: Chiitaa ga ike ni okkochiitaa.
Meaning: The cheetah fell into the pond.
Joke Explanation:
Cheetah → チーター
Fall down → 落っこちる (okkochiru)

This is more of an N2-level joke because the dramatized, colloquial form of 落ちる used in this joke isn’t commonly learned or taught early on. The rest of the rhyme uses easier vocabulary and grammar. We see が used once again as a subject particle, describing what the cheetah is doing. Combining this with the kanji for pond, 池, and using に as a preposition for the direction of the cheetah sets us up for the punchline.

The informal past tense of “to fall down” sounds just like the katakana word for cheetah, if dragged out, completing our homophonic dad joke. Once again, 落っこちる is more of a spoken, dramatized version of 落ちる
6. イルカはいるか？(iruka wa iruka?)

Romaji: Iruka wa iruka
Meaning: Are there any dolphins?
Joke Explanation:
Dolphin → イルカ
there is (living subject) → いる

This joke is as easy and cheesy as it gets. イルカ is written in katakana mainly because the kanji is hard to read, so it’s more convenient and accessible. は is used as our subject particle, as the dolphins are the subject of our silly question. いる, the word for “there is” when referring to animate subjects, is given the informal suffix か to turn it into a question. Maybe use this dad joke when you visit the Sumida Aquarium near Tokyo Skytree to test some reactions.
7. 車で、来るまで待つ。(kuruma de, kuru made matsu.)

Romaji: kuruma de kuru made matsu
Meaning: I will wait until they come by car.
Joke Explanation:
Car → 車 (kuruma)
Come → 来る (kuru)
Until → まで

Great for beginners to stretch their minds, this one uses a somewhat clever homophone, relying on the connection between 来る and まで to form the punchline. A phonetic mirror, if executed perfectly, 来るまで should sound just like 車 being enunciated poorly. 待つ is an N5-level vocabulary word meaning to wait. まで has several grammatical uses, but here it signifies waiting for the preceding action to occur.
8. 歯科医師が司会した。(shikaishi ga shikaishita)

Romaji: shikaishi ga shikaishita
Meaning: The dentist moderated the meeting
Joke Explanation:
Dentist → 歯科医師 (shikaishi)
Moderated → 司会する (shikai suru)

Because of the vocabulary it uses, this joke might be around N2 level. It’s structurally similar to the homophone examples we explained earlier, but it requires advanced kanji & vocab knowledge. This joke rests on the past tense of 司会する (shikaisuru), which is 司会した (shikaishita), meaning “led” or “moderated”.
To pull this dad joke off, you must pronounce 司会した (shikaishita) to sound exactly like 歯科医師 (shikaishita), which takes some over-enunciation of the し in した.
9. 電話に出んわ (Denwa ni denwa)

Romaji: denwa ni denwa
Meaning: I won’t answer the phone.
Explanation:
Phone → 電話 (denwa)
Answer → 出る (deru)

While the grammar and vocabulary are quite simple, the use of a different Japanese dialect could confuse beginners. This dad joke uses the Kansai dialect, which you may hear in Osaka or around Kyoto. The punchline of the joke takes the standard phrase 電話に出ない, dropping ない (nai) and adding ん (n), a shortened negative form, and the Kansai suffix わ, used to express emphasis. Now, 出ない sounds like denwa, similar to the word for “phone” or “call.”

In English, depending on where you learned to speak, we all say things a bit differently. The same applies to Japan, where different regions have their own way of saying things. One of the main alternatives to standard Japanese is the rough-sounding Kansai dialect.
10. 私はニューヨークで入浴した。(watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuuyokushita.)

Romaji: Watashi wa nyuu yooku de nyuyokushita
Meaning: I took a bath in New York.
Explanation:
Bathing (formal) → 入浴 (nyuuyoku)
New York → ニューヨーク

Although this joke is grammatically simple, the term 入浴 (nyuuyoku) is very formal and uses old kanji that you will likely only see at an onsen. If you stretch out 入浴 (nyuuyoku), it sounds like how you would pronounce New York in katakana: ニューヨーク (nyuuyooku).

Combining these two homophones with the particle で, which denotes the location of the action, means the bath was taken in New York. Onsen are where you might see this kanji used seriously, for example: 入浴時間 (nyuuyoku jikan), meaning bathing hours.
How to Make Your Own Japanese Dad Jokes
Since these jokes are great practice for your Japanese skills no matter your level, consider playing around and writing your own. Here are a few easy steps to get you started.
Pay attention to homophones. Japanese’s limited number of unique syllables naturally creates many homophones.
Use simple grammar structures. These jokes don’t require difficult grammar, so don’t be afraid to form sentences informally.
Use what you know. This is the best way to master a language; using what you have learned in your own way will lead to a strong acquisition of Japanese.
Conclusion: Dad Jokes are Great for Practicing Japanese!
Once you get the hang of these puns, it is fun to use the vocab and grammar that you are familiar with to construct your own. This is a very basic one:

Salmon roe → いくら
How much? → いくら
いくらはいくら？
How much is the salmon roe?

Expressing your sense of humor is a huge part of language learning and speaking Japanese more naturally! Jokes aren’t only fun; they can help you remember more words and express yourself more freely without sticking to rigid, literal definitions!
Sharing a laugh may be one of the best ways to practice Japanese!

Whether you’re starting from scratch or you want to take your Japanese to the next level, we have a class for you! Visit one of our campuses in Tokyo or Yokohama, or join online from anywhere around the world!

FAQ
What is oyaji gyagu?
親父ギャグ (oyaji gyagu) is the Japanese version of dad jokes. Literally meaning old man gag.
Why are dad jokes popular in Japan?
They originate from ancient poetry techniques and have been ingrained in modern comedy culture, with the added usefulness of their capability to break tension in stressful environments.
Can dad jokes help me learn Japanese?
Yes! They help you focus your listening skills for a language with so few syllables, and practice grammar by playing around with sentence structure.

items.text:
The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

While the website states the intent was to be a resource for people aiming to write in Japanese, it's helpful for Japanese learners as well. Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

パパパパパピィ

Update: Sadly this resource is no longer available.

Do you miss the good ol' days of reading picture books as a kid? Would you like to know more about Japanese children's books and the colorful images and themes they have inside? With the YouTube channel パパパパパピィ, you can read along, in a bedtime story fashion, to many different Japanese children's books.

Each story is read front to back by the host of the channel, who keeps you engaged with different voices and sounds, depending on the character or noise. You'll be able to follow along with the script, as the pages are shown while being narrated. Picture books are a great resource for beginner learners, as they don't have as many kanji. The readings are very short, witheach video being under ten minutes long. Whether you're looking to find more resources for your kids, or you're wanting to bring back the nostalgia of reading children's books, give this channel a go and watch how you're instantly transported to the land of cheery Japanese stories!

Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures

If you're wanting to get more listening practice in, the podcast Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures could be the right fit for you. This podcast was created for Japanese learners and could be used somewhat similarly to JLPT listening practice. In this podcast, the host, Megumi, talks about various experiences she's had related to travel, Japanese culture, and more. The way Megumi describes these adventures is story-like, with background music to accompany her anecdotes and detailed accounts. She speaks slowly and clearly, which is good for those who are just beginning to listen to content that's entirely in Japanese. The targeted audience for this podcast is around the intermediate level.

For listeners who would like to follow along with the dialogue, there are also transcripts on Megumi's website. At the end of these transcripts, there are English translations for some of the more advanced vocabulary. The episodes are around 5 minutes in length, so they're quick listens if you want to give them a go.

Human Japanese

Made by the same people who brought us Satori Reader, the Human Japanese apps are basically digital textbooks for Japanese, or as they call it, your "personal sensei in a box." There is an app for beginners and then an intermediate-level version. The beginner version boasts over 500 pages of content and around 800 example sentences, with breakdowns of each word and particle to boot! When teaching kana and kanji, there are stroke order animations, and plenty of example words as well.

The lessons in this app are truly worded and organized like a textbook. You will find lessons related to food, school, geography, health, work, and the weather. Major grammar points are included as well, including lessons on verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjugations, counting, particles, and more. At the end of each lesson, you can find review quizzes. By default, you cannot move on to the next chapter until you have passed a chapter review quiz, but you can change this in the settings.

The overall design of the app is sleek and nice, but can feel a little dated to some seeing as it was originally created over a decade ago. Some pages are a little intimidating because of their word count, which some may find annoying. And there are no romaji to help you out; the app assumes you will learn hiragana and katakana. So if this kind of electronic textbook is just what you're looking for, then Human Japanese may be for you. For readers looking to give it a try, they offer a lite version free of charge.

YomuJP

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.

YomuJP
https://files.tofugu.com/japanese-learning-resources-database/yomujp/yomujp.jpg

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.

items.author: Coto Academy Staff Writer
items.summary: If you’ve registered for the JLPT and hit the point where self-study isn’t cutting it anymore, you’ve probably already started searching for a JLPT prep
items.text:
If you’ve registered for the JLPT and hit the point where self-study isn’t cutting it anymore, you’ve probably already started searching for a JLPT prep course. And that search gets harder fast if you’re taking the exam outside Japan or hoping to study online.

While there are plenty of online Japanese lessons out there, there are surprisingly few actual JLPT-focused courses. Even when you find one, there’s still the matter of finding a class with the right schedule: navigating time zones and pricing structures that aren’t always clear upfront.

So we did the legwork. Below are the best JLPT online courses available right now, with pricing, pros, cons, and what to weigh before you commit.

How Are JLPT Courses Different from Regular Japanese Courses?

So what’s the difference between a JLPT course and a regular Japanese course?

The short answer: a regular Japanese course teaches you to use the language; a JLPT course teaches you to pass a specific test. They overlap, but their priorities are different.

Regular courses (like Coto Academy’s typical Japanese lessons) are built around speaking and practical use. You’re learning to hold a conversation, order food, get through a job interview, and get that transfer to daily life in Japan. They don’t map cleanly onto how the JLPT actually tests you.

JLPT courses are built around one goal: passing the JLPT. On the content side, JLPT courses lean into grammar and analytical reading, which most conversation-based courses skip entirely, since it has little to do with speaking ability but a lot to do with passing.

On the practice side, expect regular mock tests under timed conditions rather than casual exercises, so you get used to the actual pacing before test day. And layered around all of that are exam-specific tips. Since it is usually taught by JLPT instructors, you will get tips like how to eliminate wrong answers fast, how to budget your time per section, and how question types tend to repeat across past exams.

Best JLPT Online Course

CourseLevelDurationBest For

Coto AcademyN3–N11 year or 6 months (flexible)Learners who want live instruction with flexible scheduling and the option to focus on specific sections (grammar/reading vs. kanji/vocab)

J-StandardN5–N1FlexibleSelf-paced learners who want structure without a live class schedule. Good for beginners through upper-intermediate

PreplyFlexibleFlexibleLearners who want fully personalized 1-on-1 tutoring and don’t mind vetting tutors themselves

SNGN3, N23 monthsLearners who want a short, all-around intensive with a final practice exam

Kudan InstituteN3–N12 monthsLearners near Japan-friendly time zones who want a short, grammar-only review.

Japonin (JOI)N1–N4 (N5 private)Flexible (book lesson by lesson)Learners outside Japan who need scheduling flexibility over a fixed cohort

Coto Academy

Best for: Learners who want live instruction with flexible scheduling and the option to focus on specific sections (grammar/reading vs. kanji/vocab).

Available levelJLPT N3 to N1

Duration1 year or 6 months

PricePoint-based subscription. Each lesson costs 2 points. The recommended plan is 16 points per 28 days at ¥16,800, or 8 points per 28 days at ¥9,600 on the monthly plan.

HighlightsJLPT lessons tailored to your focus area, flexible scheduling, and instruction taught only by professional instructors.

Coto Academy offers a fully online JLPT preparation course through its learning platform, online.cotoacademy.com. You purchase lesson points and can book a class immediately.

The course is currently offered at the N3 and N1 levels, with two format options.

The one-year course focuses on grammar and reading, and you can join anytime. It’s built for steady, ongoing progress and includes interactive exercises throughout, which makes it useful even if you’re not specifically preparing for the JLPT.

The six-month course is split into two tracks: grammar and reading, or kanji and vocabulary. This one is lecture-style and designed to support self-study. Classes are taught primarily through instructor explanations in a group Zoom session, where students can ask and answer questions through chat. Through this course, you’ll watch instructors break down key vocabulary, expressions, and problem-solving strategies for each level, then practice with questions formatted just like the real JLPT.

Because the course is divided by test section, you can customize your prep. If you’re already covering vocabulary through something like Anki, you can skip that track and focus only on grammar and reading.


Contact Us and Start Learning Japanese!


J-Standard

Best for: Self-paced learners who want structure without a live class schedule.

Available levelJLPT N5 to N1

DurationFlexible

Price$69/3 months, or $180/year

Highlights1,200+ lessons and quizzes, real-world dialogues, teacher-led, on-demand video instruction

J-Standard is built for learners who want steady, structured progress without being tied to a class schedule.

It’s not a live online JLPT course, but that’s kind of the point. If you’ve ever sat down to study JLPT by yourself and had no idea where to start or what to focus on next, J-Standard takes that guesswork off your plate. It walks you step by step through every unit and level, so instead of piecing together your own study plan from scratch, you just follow the path. It covers everything from hiragana and katakana through N5 to N2 grammar and vocabulary, all in one platform, all at your own pace.

The learning journey follows four steps. You start by watching teacher-led videos to learn new grammar and vocabulary, then apply it through real, practical dialogues based on everyday situations in Japan.

From there, you move into JLPT-style drills and quizzes to lock in what you’ve learned, and track it all on a simple dashboard that keeps your study hours and progress visible.

Currently, the platform has over 1,200 lessons and quizzes covering grammar, vocabulary, listening, and reading. We recommend it if you want something affordable and flexible enough to fit into a busy schedule, without sacrificing structure.

Get a 14-day Free Trial

Preply

Best for: Learners who want fully personalized 1-on-1 tutoring and don’t mind doing some legwork to find the right tutor.

Available levelFlexible

DurationFlexible

Price$20 – 70/hour, depending on tutor

HighlightsPersonalized plan since it is typically 1-on-1 tutoring, but not always with professional instructors

You’ve probably already heard of Preply, a language platform that connects you with independent tutors. You can find tutors who specialize in JLPT prep and build a lesson plan around your specific goals.

The trade-off is consistency. Most tutors are native speakers, but not all of them are trained instructors, so teaching quality and JLPT-specific expertise can vary a lot from one tutor to the next. If you go this route, we recommend reading reviews and trying a few tutors before committing, since the experience depends on who you end up with.

Pricing varies and isn’t always affordable. Preply’s community tutors, meaning native speakers without formal certification, typically run $20 to $40 an hour. However, certified instructors cost more, usually $40 to $70 an hour, which adds up fast for private, one-on-one sessions.

The great thing is that because Preply usually only does 1-on-1 tutoring, it can work well if you want maximum flexibility and don’t mind doing some legwork to find the right fit, but it’s a less structured option compared to a dedicated JLPT platform like Coto Academy or J-Standard.

Want to double your chances of passing JLPT? Join Coto Academy!

Inquire Now

SNG

Best for: Learners who already have a Japanese base and want a short, all-around intensive with a final practice exam.

Available levelJLPT N3 and N2

Duration3 months, 30 hours across 10 lessons

Price¥39,600 for new students

HighlightsAll-around JLPT prep course on a short duration

SNG’s Online JLPT Preparation Course covers all test sections: vocabulary, kanji, grammar, reading comprehension, and listening. Lessons use digital content to track your understanding as you go, and instructors focus extra time on whatever you’re struggling with most. You’ll get 30 hours of class time across 10 lessons, wrapping up with a final practice exam to confirm you’re ready for test day.

By the end of the course, you’ll have mastered the vocabulary, grammar, and kanji needed to pass the JLPT, built the listening skills to comprehend short conversations, and picked up test-taking strategies and tips to boost your overall score.

Note that this course isn’t for beginners. You’ll need at least 300 study hours of Japanese under your belt before enrolling in N3, or 600 hours for N2.

Want to study Japanese with us?

Inquire Now

Kudan Japanese Institute

Best for: Learners in Japan-friendly time zones who want a short, grammar-only review before test day.

Available levelJLPT N3 to N1

Duration2 months

Price¥49,500

HighlightsAll-around JLPT prep course in a short duration

Kudan Institute takes a narrower approach than most JLPT courses on this list: it covers grammar only. Rather than splitting attention across vocabulary, reading, and listening, the course drills grammar patterns intensively over a six-week run, timed right before the JLPT exam.

The structure centers on pattern recognition. Grammar questions are broken down and sorted into recognizable question types, so instead of memorizing textbook entries in isolation, you learn to spot what a question is actually testing. Each session pairs that analysis with strategy review, and then interactive practice with the target grammar so it doesn’t stay theoretical.

Enrollment is open mid-course, so joining in week three is a genuine option if you’ve only just realized grammar is your weak point.

The catch is that lessons run in the evening Japan time on weekdays. If you’re in Europe or the Americas, evening JST lands in your morning on a workday: early morning for much of Europe and the middle of the night for parts of North America.

Japonin

Best for: Learners outside Japan who need scheduling flexibility more than they need a fixed cohort.

Available levelJLPT N1 to N4 (N5 via private lessons)

DurationFlexible — book lesson by lesson

PriceFrom ¥1,280 per lesson (group) / ¥3,380 per lesson (private)

HighlightsAll-around JLPT prep with bookable time slots and 2 free trial lessons

Best for: Learners outside Japan who need scheduling flexibility more than they need a fixed cohort.

Japonin’s online JLPT space. Classes run on Zoom in 50-minute blocks with a maximum of seven students, and teachers average around 15 years of experience.

Group classes cover N1 through N4, with N5 handled through private lessons. Rather than focusing on grammar alone, the curriculum integrates grammar, vocabulary, kanji, reading, and listening, with grammar as the backbone, which suits learners who want their JLPT prep to double as general language study rather than pure exam drilling.

Instead of committing to a fixed weekly slot, you book each class individually from multiple time options each week, so the course bends around a shifting work schedule or an awkward time zone, not the other way around. Most lessons use Japonin’s own slides built from classroom experience rather than a commercial textbook, with published materials reserved for the final prep courses. Pricing sits at roughly ¥1,280–¥1,320 per lesson for small-group FlexLessons and from ¥3,380 for private one-on-one, and you can take up to two free 50-minute trial lessons at any level before committing.

Unfortunately, that same flexibility means no cohort moves through a syllabus alongside you, so you’re responsible for building a consistent study rhythm.

Want to study JLPT online? Join Coto Academy!

Inquire Now

Ready to Start Your JLPT Prep?

Of all the options on this list, Coto Academy’s JLPT course is the one built to flex around you. Whether you want a full year of steady grammar and reading practice or a focused six-month sprint through the exact sections you’re weakest in, you pick the format, book lessons instantly with points, and learn from instructors who teach JLPT prep professionally — not tutors picking it up on the side.

If you’re serious about passing, don’t leave your prep to a platform that treats JLPT as an afterthought. Start with a course that was actually built for the exam.


Contact Us and Start Learning Japanese!


FAQ

What is the best JLPT online course?

It depends on what you need. Coto Academy is the strongest all-around pick if you want live instruction, professional JLPT instructors, and flexible scheduling. J-Standard is best if you want a self-paced, affordable option without live classes. Preply suits learners who want 1-on-1 tutoring and are willing to vet tutors themselves. There’s no single “best” course for everyone — the right one depends on your level, budget, time zone, and whether you want live or self-paced instruction.


Are JLPT online courses actually effective?

Yes, as long as the course is built around the exam rather than general conversation. A good JLPT course gives you timed mock tests, exam-specific strategy, and focused practice on the sections the real test weights heavily, like grammar and reading — things self-study and conversation-based classes typically don’t cover in depth.


How long does it take to prepare for the JLPT with an online course?

It varies by level and course. Short intensives like Kudan Institute or SNG run 2–3 months and are designed as a final push before the exam. Longer programs like Coto Academy’s one-year track suit learners building proficiency from the ground up. As a rule, the higher the level (N2, N1), the more prep time you should budget.

How much do JLPT online courses cost?

Pricing ranges widely: J-Standard starts around $69 for 3 months, Japonin runs from about ¥1,280 per lesson, and structured short-term intensives like SNG or Kudan run roughly ¥39,600–¥49,500 for a 2–3 month course. Live 1-on-1 tutoring through Preply is the most expensive per hour ($20–$70), since you’re paying for individual attention.

Do I need to already know Japanese to join a JLPT online course?

Most courses assume some prior study. J-Standard is the exception, starting from hiragana and katakana for true beginners. Others, like SNG, require a minimum number of self-study hours (300+ for N3, 600+ for N2) before enrolling.

Pricing ranges widely: J-Standard starts around $69 for 3 months, Japonin runs from about ¥1,280 per lesson, and structured short-term intensives like SNG or Kudan run roughly ¥39,600–¥49,500 for a 2–3 month course. Live 1-on-1 tutoring through Preply is the most expensive per hour ($20–$70), since you’re paying for individual attention.
Do I need to already know Japanese to join a JLPT online course?

Most courses assume some prior study. J-Standard is the exception, starting from hiragana and katakana for true beginners. Others, like SNG, require a minimum number of self-study hours (300+ for N3, 600+ for N2) before enrolling.

items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In
items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.

items.text:
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the lesbian bar mask mandate implosion.

When did we stop throwing dinner parties? According to some recent polls surfaced by The Atlantic, rates have been declining for years. The larger context, with which you may already be familiar, is the loneliness epidemic; the slow tightening of our social circles, the dissolving of our web of relationships both casual and intimate. Fewer gatherings like dinner parties offer less opportunities to nurture these relationships. Fewer close relationships make corralling friends for a dinner party all the more difficult.

But it’s not all doom and gloom. As I reported a couple years ago, some Gen Z’ers are throwing friend-making dinner parties in their own homes. Be the change you want to see in the world. Bake a cake and invite your friends over to eat it with you!

Also in today’s Open Tab: DoorDash unveils new programming, we dip a toe into the $60 rye discourse, more restaurant critics bring back stars, and the psychiatrists prescribing GLP-1s for mental health.

DoorDash Leans in to the AI Rat Race

Last week delivery platform DoorDash paid out an historic $131.5 million settlement to New York City delivery workers. This week it debuted a new text-based AI platform through which you can order groceries and restaurant delivery. The platform builds on the recent uptick of other text-based AI-agents like Instinct and Meta’s Muse. You can sign up for the waiting list to test it in beta, but when I reached out to DoorDash to ask how many people were on the waiting list, all a spokesperson would tell me is that the company is “excited by the early interest we’re seeing.”

Also notable: DoorDash announced a pilot program for autonomous delivery drones in Northern California, partnering with restaurants like Chipotle and Popeyes. Will this program expand to eventually take the jobs of human delivery workers? According to a spokesperson, these drones will be used for a “specific use case—mid-range, time-sensitive, small payload,” and “drones are adding capacity for a specific slice of orders, not pulling volume away from Dashers.”

As the tech evolves, though, it’s hard to imagine the company won’t favor drones and robots to which they will never have to worry about paying out a settlement of more than a hundred million dollars over wage issues.

I ate the $60 loaf of rye so you don’t have to

Much has been made of the new bakery, Rye, by Martin Auer, which opened in New York City’s SoHo almost exactly three weeks ago. It serves just one item: a 3-pound loaf of rye bread made with imported Austrian rye flour. (And, okay, a number of tartines.) The hullabaloo is around the price: $60 per loaf in New York, compared to the mere 14 Euros around Austria, where Auer runs a chain of these bakeries.

Auer has received a decent amount of blowback online. Even grocery chain Lidl clowned the shop publicly. Does Auer deserve the hate? I mean, if you don’t want to buy the bread, just don’t buy the bread, right?

For what it’s worth, when I went to the bakery to talk to Martin’s son Tim, with whom he runs the bakery, he told me the bread is priced to cover the cost of importing the flour, the labor, the size of the loaf—three pounds!—and, notably, the monthly rent on a space in SoHo which, if comparable store fronts are any measure, would likely measure into the several tens of thousands.

The younger Auer also told me the bakery is selling out often, though he wouldn’t specify how many loaves per day are made; he opaquely suggested somewhere between 50 and 300.

Was the bread good? Yeah, it was fine. Kind of dense, nutty, and overall pretty mild in flavor. Was it worth sixty American dollars? To me, it seems steep for any loaf of bread, but as we talked about last week, everything is a luxury item now. It’s all priced accordingly.

The new (old) rules for restaurant critics

Decades ago, we had a clear picture of who restaurant critics were. Among them, Mimi Sheraton, who donned wigs and other disguises to go unrecognized when reviewing. Jonathan Gold expanded readers’ minds by unearthing small hidden gems serving thrilling food. Sometimes they were Anton Ego, probably the most widely known (though fictitious) food critic from Disney’s Ratatouille, who seemed to love writing cruel reviews solely for sport.

In the last few years, newspaper restaurant critics have been rewriting the rules of the game. Though New York magazine’s former critic, Adam Platt, famously dropped anonymity way back in 2013, the first newspaper critic to unmask themself was Alison Cook of the Houston Chronicle in 2012; even Gold unmasked himself in 2015. The major reveals remained quiet for some time, and then since 2019, critics like Soleil Ho (San Francisco Chronicle), Lyndsay C. Green (Detroit Free Press), and Louisa Kung Liu Chu (Chicago Tribune) dropped the performance of anonymity upon taking on the mantle at their respective publications. Only last year, critics at the Los Angeles Times, The New York Times, and The Washington Post followed suit.

This is all to say that restaurant criticism is always adapting with the times.

One such policy, the starred review, has been a subject of debate for many papers still publishing restaurant reviews. During the 2020 COVID pandemic, many legacy newspapers paused or retired their starred reviews out of respect for the restaurants and their workers suffering from debilitatingly slow business during the lockdown. Fast-forward to today as publications bring back those same starred ratings. In an era dominated by food and restaurant influencers, the argument the critics (and their editors) make is that star ratings help to give a definitive delineation to restaurant reviews written by true experts in the field.

Hilary, a 39-year-old in California, has had depression for about as long as she can remember, which means she’s tried a lot of antidepressants. Mostly, though, the meds left her unimpressed. Then she began taking a GLP-1. A few months in, she felt like her entire outlook had become more positive.

Hilary’s case isn’t wholly unique. Growing evidence shows that GLP-1s may relieve some symptoms of depression. That’s led psychiatrists to use it as a tool in conjunction with nutritional therapy on their patients. Read on to see how GLP-1s have made it to the therapy couch.

Hilary’s case isn’t wholly unique. Growing evidence shows that GLP-1s may relieve some symptoms of depression. That’s led psychiatrists to use it as a tool in conjunction with nutritional therapy on their patients. Read on to see how GLP-1s have made it to the therapy couch.
